chapter: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
title: Illinois Jacquet's rhythm section and joining his octet at the Apollo
summary: He had furnished Jacquet a rhythm section earlier, and in January 1948 replaces Sir Charles Thompson in the Jacquet group.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: So anyway, I left and I came back to Washington. I had been here about I guess three weeks, maybe a month... No, it wasn't, it was about three weeks. And I got this call from Illinois Jacquet. I had met him earlier, right after I had left the Eckstine band, because around that same time he had just left the Basie band, and he came down to Washington by himself. He came down and he contacted me to get a rhythm section for him, which I got myself, I got Tommy Potter, and I think the drummer was this same fellow, Charlie Buck I believe. Yeah, Charlie Buck, Tommy Potter and myself -- and Illinois. And Leo Parker was here then, because he had left the Eckstine band, and Leo came up with his baritone and sat in with... Oh, there was another one, Joe Newman. Joe Newman and Illinois came down together. So I furnished the rhythm section for them. And of course, Leo Parker came up and played baritone. And they had a very successful dance.

So this was a kind of a feeler for Illinois, I guess, for the record people and agents to find out what kind of drawing power he had. Because he had been with the Basie band and with Lionel Hampton, "Flying Home" and all that, and also Cab Calloway. So he went back and he formed this eight-piece

group, which had Joe Newman and his brother Russell on trumpet. He had Shadow Wilson on drums. He sent and got Leo Parker, who played baritone saxophone. And he had a bass player named Al Lucas who had formerly played with Duke Ellington and I remember with a band called the Sunset Royals Entertainers, which was quite a band back in the Thirties. And he had Sir Charles Thompson on piano. Which made up the group. And the band was doing great.

They had been together I guess about two or three months. And right after I left Billy Eckstine as his accompanist, about three weeks later, in early 1948, I think about the last week in January, I got this call from Illinois. He was going into the Apollo Theatre, and he needed a pianist. I asked him what had happened to Sir Charles -- because I knew Sir Charles. He said that Sir Charles had quit. So I needed a job and the money was good, he was offering me good money -- so I went and joined the band.
